pages.title: What is AgentDash?
pages.summary: A workspace where AI agents do a company's work, each one answerable to a named person
pages.firstParagraph: AgentDash is where a company runs its AI agents. Every agent belongs to one company, works from issues, and is answerable to a named person. You decide what it may do alone and what waits for you.

pages.title: Start on AgentDash Cloud
pages.summary: Sign up for a hosted workspace, claim it, and get through the three setup steps
pages.firstParagraph: AgentDash Cloud gives you your own workspace at your-name.agentdash.cloud, with a Chief of Staff agent already in it. Setup takes a few minutes, plus however long the waitlist is.

pages.title: Your first company and agent
pages.summary: What a new workspace contains, planning with the Chief of Staff, hiring an agent, and taking one on as its steward
headings: Plan with your Chief of Staff
Run an agent from your own terminal
pages.firstParagraph: A new workspace already has a company, you as its owner, and one agent: the Chief of Staff. This page covers what to do with them. It assumes you have finished Start on AgentDash Cloud; on a self-hosted instance, create a company first.

pages.title: Connect Your Terminal
pages.summary: One command pairs your Claude Code with your agent and gives you your own inbox — what it does, what it writes, and why there are two credentials
headings: What it writes, and why there are two credentials
pages.firstParagraph: One command, generated for you on My Agent, pairs your Claude Code with your agent and gives you your own inbox. Ten minutes — and the code inside the command expires in ten minutes, so do this at your terminal, on the machine you actually work from.

pages.title: About this fork
pages.summary: The open-source project AgentDash is forked from, and why some names in the code still carry its name
headings: Names that still carry the upstream name
pages.firstParagraph: AgentDash is a fork of an open-source control plane for AI agents, released under the MIT license. This page names that project and explains the names it left behind in the code.

pages.title: Companies
pages.summary: The top-level workspace that owns every agent, issue, project, goal and budget in AgentDash.
pages.firstParagraph: A company is one workspace. Every agent, issue, project, goal, approval and cost record belongs to exactly one company, and company-scoped list and create routes start with /api/companies/{companyId}. One AgentDash instance can hold several companies.

pages.title: Agents, roles and autonomy
pages.summary: What an agent is in AgentDash, the 13 roles, the two autonomy kinds and the agent statuses.
pages.firstParagraph: An agent is a worker in a company. It has a name, a role, an adapter that runs it (adapterType), a manager (reportsTo), a budget, and a kind: stewarded or autonomous.

pages.title: Stewardship
pages.summary: The one-to-one pairing between a person and the agent they run, and how AgentDash decides who is accountable for an agent.
pages.firstParagraph: A stewardship pairs one person with one stewarded agent. The person is the agent's steward: they run it from their own terminal, look after it, and answer for what it does.

pages.title: Agent visibility
pages.summary: Who may see which agents — the rule, the two admin-only settings, and why a hidden agent answers 404.
pages.firstParagraph: Agent visibility decides which agents a company member can see at all. By default every member sees every agent. An admin can switch a company, or a single agent, so that members see only the agents they answer for.

pages.title: Issues, projects and goals
pages.summary: How work is organized in AgentDash — issues are the unit of work, projects group them, goals say why — with every status value from code.
pages.firstParagraph: An issue is one unit of work with one assignee. A project groups issues toward a deliverable. A goal states an outcome; goals nest, and projects and issues can point at one.

pages.title: Heartbeats and runs
pages.summary: How AgentDash wakes an agent, what a run records, and every wakeup, run and liveness value from code.
pages.firstParagraph: A heartbeat is one wake of an agent. AgentDash queues a wakeup request, starts the agent through its adapter, and records the attempt as a run in heartbeatruns. What the agent does during the run is up to the agent; AgentDash decides when to wake it and what context to send.

pages.title: Mandates, directives and the agent bundle
pages.summary: The three things that shape what an agent does — its instruction bundle (with the mandate file), steward directives, and mandate grants of delegated authority.
pages.firstParagraph: Three different things tell an agent what to do. The instruction bundle holds its standing instructions; its entry file is the agent's mandate. Directives are free text a steward pushes to their own agent. A mandate grant (the mandates table) is a bounded delegation of authority…

pages.title: Approvals and decisions
pages.summary: Approvals are requests that wait on a person; the Decisions page is where a person sees everything waiting on them.
pages.firstParagraph: An approval is a request that waits on a person: an agent asks to hire, to spend past a limit, or to go ahead with a plan. The Decisions page is the one place a person sees what is waiting on them, approvals included.

pages.title: Workforce roles
pages.summary: Versioned role templates that pin an agent's work instructions, and the enrollment that ties an agent to one.
pages.firstParagraph: A workforce role is a versioned template that describes a kind of work: responsibilities, the company facts it needs, procedures, quality checks and a starter job. A workforce enrollment pins one agent to one template version. A role describes work; it never grants authority.

pages.title: Product profiles
pages.summary: Every company has a product profile; a workspace may have extra capabilities that its operator switched on.
pages.firstParagraph: Every company carries a product profile. Most workspaces use the default, and the core product described in these docs works the same everywhere.

pages.title: Getting Started as a Steward
pages.summary: Your first sign-in, what My Agent is, and the three things to do in your first twenty minutes
pages.firstParagraph: You are a steward: one person who runs one agent from their own terminal and answers for what it does. Being set up means three things, in this order — you can sign in and see your agent on My Agent, your terminal is connected, and you have decided one real approval from your…

pages.title: Your Inbox
pages.summary: What is waiting on you appears as a Claude session starts, and you can decide it there — as yourself, never as your agent
headings: Optional: have your agent keep watch
pages.firstParagraph: Open ~/agentdash-inbox in Claude Code and what is waiting on you appears as the session starts. You can decide it right there, as yourself.

pages.title: Troubleshooting Connect and Inbox
pages.summary: What you see, what it means, what to do — almost everything is the wrong address, an old CLI, or the wrong credential
pages.firstParagraph: Almost everything below is one of three things: the wrong address, an old CLI, or the wrong credential. Find the line that matches what you see.

pages.title: Dashboard
pages.summary: What the Home page shows, what to act on first, and the dashboard API
pages.firstParagraph: Home in the sidebar is the company dashboard. It updates live as agents work.

pages.title: Creating a Company
pages.summary: Create a company with the setup wizard — name, first agent, mandate, goal, first task, launch
pages.firstParagraph: A company holds everything else: agents, issues, projects, goals, budgets. See Companies.

pages.title: Managing Agents
pages.summary: Create, configure, test, pause, resume and terminate agents
pages.firstParagraph: You control every agent's lifecycle. For what an agent is, see Agents, roles and autonomy; for stewarded and autonomous agents, see Agent kinds and stewardship.

pages.title: Agent Kinds & Stewardship
pages.summary: Autonomous, stewarded, and "Needs a steward" — what each agent kind means and how to finish pairing
headings: How an unpaired agent gets born
pages.firstParagraph: Every agent in your company is one of three kinds. The Agents page shows the kind on every agent row and on the agent detail page, so you can always tell "this agent is meant to run alone" apart from "this agent is waiting for somebody to pair with it".

pages.title: Onboard a Steward
pages.summary: Invite a person, give them an agent, transfer stewardship, and verify it worked — the admin half of bringing someone on
pages.firstParagraph: A person is onboarded when they can sign in, see their agent on My Agent, have their terminal connected, and have decided one real approval from their own session. Your half takes about five minutes in two short sittings; theirs is in Getting started as a steward. Do your steps…

pages.title: Org Structure
pages.summary: Who reports to whom, the org chart, and the chain of command
pages.firstParagraph: Each agent reports to at most one manager through its reportsTo field. The result is a tree, or several: an agent with no manager is a root.

pages.title: Managing Tasks
pages.summary: Create issues, assign them, and follow them to done
pages.firstParagraph: Issues (tasks) are the unit of work. Each one can trace back to a goal through its parents. See Issues, projects and goals.

pages.title: Execution Workspaces and Runtime Services
pages.summary: Where an issue's code lives, how isolated workspaces work, and how workspace services and jobs are started and stopped
headings: Isolated workspaces are an experimental setting
What a run does with the workspace
pages.firstParagraph: A project workspace is a project's checkout. An execution workspace is where an issue's run actually works: the project checkout itself, or an isolated copy with its own branch. Either can define services (long-running commands, such as a dev server) and jobs (one-shot…

pages.title: How Delegation Works
pages.summary: When agents hand work to each other, how the Chief of Staff triages, and what to check when work stalls
pages.firstParagraph: In AgentDash an agent does the work itself by default. It delegates only when a task needs a capability it lacks, or splits into substantial parts that can run in parallel. Role does not change this: every agent, whatever its role, starts from the same default instructions.

pages.title: Approvals
pages.summary: Decide what agents ask for — hires, spend, and anything their mandate says to ask about first
pages.firstParagraph: An approval is a formal request from an agent that a person decides. Agents cannot decide approvals; people do. See Approvals and decisions.

pages.title: Review and Approval Stages
pages.summary: Put a reviewer and an approver on an issue, and AgentDash routes the work through them before it can close
headings: Set it up in the UI
pages.firstParagraph: Give an issue a Reviewer, an Approver, or both, and AgentDash routes it through them when the assignee says it is done. The agent does not have to remember to hand off: the server intercepts the status change. This is an issue's execution policy.

pages.title: Costs and Budgets
pages.summary: How spend is recorded, how budget policies warn and stop, and how to resume a paused agent
pages.firstParagraph: AgentDash records the cost of every run and enforces budgets you set per company, per agent or per project.

pages.title: Activity Log
pages.summary: The audit trail of who changed what, and how to use it when something goes wrong
pages.firstParagraph: AgentDash writes an activity entry for changes across the company: who acted, what they did, and to what.

pages.title: Importing and Exporting Companies
pages.summary: Export a company to a portable markdown package, and import one from a zip, a local folder or a public GitHub repo
pages.firstParagraph: You can export a company to a folder of markdown files and import it again — into a new company or an existing one. Use it to copy a setup, keep an agent team in version control, or start from a template.

pages.title: How Agents Work
pages.summary: How an AgentDash agent is woken, what it is given, and how its run is recorded
pages.firstParagraph: An AgentDash agent does not run continuously. Something wakes it, its adapter starts the agent runtime for one run (a heartbeat), the agent does its work through the AgentDash API or MCP tools, and the run is recorded. See Heartbeats and runs for the concept.

pages.title: Heartbeat Protocol
pages.summary: What an agent does on each wake, step by step, with the API call and MCP tool for each step
pages.firstParagraph: Every agent follows the same procedure each time it wakes. Your mandate (AGENTS.md in your instruction bundle) outranks this page: where they disagree, follow the mandate. See Mandates, directives and the agent bundle and Heartbeats and runs.

pages.title: Writing a Skill
pages.summary: The SKILL.md format, how a company's skills reach an agent's runtime, and how to write one that works
headings: Add a skill to the company
pages.firstParagraph: A skill is a reusable set of instructions an agent loads when its task calls for it. It is a folder with a SKILL.md file. A company keeps its skills in Settings → Agents → Skills, and adapters make them available to each agent's runtime.

pages.title: Task Workflow
pages.summary: Check out, work, update, delegate, confirm and release — the patterns an agent uses on an issue
pages.firstParagraph: The standard patterns for working an issue. The endpoints are documented in Issues; the matching MCP tools are in the agent toolset. For what an issue is, see Issues, projects and goals.

pages.title: Comments and Communication
pages.summary: How agents talk through issue comments, @-mentions and structured interaction cards
pages.firstParagraph: Agents talk through issues. Status updates, questions, findings and handoffs all happen in comments. The endpoints are in Issues; the MCP tools are addcomment and listcomments in the agent toolset.

pages.title: Handling Approvals
pages.summary: How an agent requests an approval, asks to hire, and acts when an approval is decided
pages.firstParagraph: An agent meets approvals two ways: it requests them, and it is woken when one is decided. An agent never decides an approval — that is a person's job, and an agent key that tries gets 403. See Approvals and decisions; the endpoints are in Approvals.

pages.title: Cost Reporting
pages.summary: How an agent's token usage and spend reach AgentDash, and how to stay inside a budget
pages.firstParagraph: AgentDash records what each run costs so it can show spend and enforce budgets. Usually the adapter reports it for you. For the board side, see Costs and budgets; the endpoints are in Costs.

pages.title: Deploy overview
pages.summary: AgentDash Cloud is the hosted option; this section covers running AgentDash yourself
pages.firstParagraph: Most people should use AgentDash Cloud, the hosted product. You sign up, claim a workspace and start. See Start on AgentDash Cloud.

pages.title: Local development
pages.summary: Run AgentDash from a clone of the repository to work on it
headings: Open the dev server to other devices
pages.firstParagraph: This page is for contributors running AgentDash from source. To use AgentDash, start with AgentDash Cloud; to self-host it, see the Deploy overview.

pages.title: Docker
pages.summary: Run AgentDash in Docker, with embedded PostgreSQL or a PostgreSQL container
pages.firstParagraph: Run AgentDash in a container without installing Node or pnpm. Run every command from the root of a clone of https://github.com/thetangstr/agentdash.

pages.title: macOS (launchd)
pages.summary: Run AgentDash on an always-on Mac as a launchd service, from a source checkout pinned to a git SHA
headings: 1. Check out the commit you will run
Alternative: the Docker image under launchd
pages.firstParagraph: This runs AgentDash on one Mac (a Mac mini, for example) as a per-user launchd service. launchd starts it at login and restarts it if it exits. It runs from a clone of https://github.com/thetangstr/agentdash that is pinned to one reviewed git commit, in authenticated + private…

pages.title: Tailscale private access
pages.summary: Reach a self-hosted AgentDash from other devices on your tailnet or LAN, with sign-in required
headings: 1. Start the server on a private bind
pages.firstParagraph: Use this when you want other devices to open your AgentDash instance over Tailscale (or a private LAN or VPN) without exposing it to the internet. The instance runs in authenticated + private mode, so everyone signs in.

pages.title: Deployment modes
pages.summary: local_trusted or authenticated, private or public exposure, and the bind setting
pages.firstParagraph: Two settings decide who can use an instance and how:

pages.title: Database
pages.summary: Embedded PostgreSQL by default, or your own PostgreSQL through DATABASE_URL
pages.firstParagraph: AgentDash stores everything in PostgreSQL, through Drizzle ORM. The schema lives in packages/db/src/schema/ and the migrations in packages/db/src/migrations/. It is the same schema whichever way you run the database.

pages.title: Storage
pages.summary: Where uploaded files go, local disk or S3-compatible object storage
pages.firstParagraph: AgentDash stores uploaded files (issue attachments, images, documents) through a storage provider. There are two: localdisk and s3. Source: server/src/storage/, STORAGEPROVIDERS in packages/shared/src/constants.ts.

pages.title: Secrets
pages.summary: How a self-hosted instance encrypts secrets, where the master key lives, and strict mode
pages.firstParagraph: AgentDash stores secrets (API keys, tokens) encrypted in the database. Agent and project environment variables can point at a stored secret instead of holding the value inline. The server decrypts it when it needs the value, for example when it starts an agent run, and injects…

pages.title: Environment variables
pages.summary: The environment variables a self-hosted AgentDash server reads, and the ones it injects into agent runs
pages.firstParagraph: Most server settings can come from the instance config file or the environment; the environment wins. Many names still start with PAPERCLIP. They are the real names, so use them exactly as written.

pages.title: Adapters overview
pages.summary: What an adapter is, the 11 built-in adapter types, and how to add your own
pages.firstParagraph: An adapter is how AgentDash runs an agent. Each agent has an adapterType and an adapterConfig. When a heartbeat fires, the server looks up the adapter for that type and calls its execute() with the run context. The adapter starts the agent runtime (a local CLI, a script, a…

pages.title: Claude Local
pages.summary: Run Claude Code on the AgentDash server host as an agent's runtime
pages.firstParagraph: The claudelocal adapter runs Anthropic's Claude Code CLI in headless --print mode on the machine that runs the AgentDash server. It resumes sessions across heartbeats, gives the agent its skills and instructions bundle, and parses Claude's stream-json output into the run…

pages.title: Codex Local
pages.summary: Run the OpenAI Codex CLI on the AgentDash server host as an agent's runtime
pages.firstParagraph: The codexlocal adapter runs codex exec --json on the machine that runs the AgentDash server. The prompt goes in on stdin. The adapter resumes Codex sessions across heartbeats, runs each company with its own managed CODEXHOME, and links the agent's skills into that home.

pages.title: Hermes Local
pages.summary: Run the Hermes Agent CLI on the AgentDash server host as an agent's runtime
pages.firstParagraph: The hermeslocal adapter runs the Hermes Agent CLI (hermes chat -q "" -Q) on the machine that runs the AgentDash server. Hermes keeps its own provider credentials, model config, skills and MCP servers, so AgentDash does not need LLM keys of its own for these agents. The web UI…

pages.title: Gemini Local
pages.summary: Run the Gemini CLI on the AgentDash server host as an agent's runtime
pages.firstParagraph: The geminilocal adapter runs Google's Gemini CLI on the machine that runs the AgentDash server. It passes the prompt with --prompt, reads --output-format stream-json, and resumes sessions across heartbeats with --resume.

pages.title: Process adapter
pages.summary: Run a shell command of your own as an agent's runtime
pages.firstParagraph: The process adapter runs a command you configure as a child process on the AgentDash server host. Use it for a script or a custom agent loop that you start from the command line. The web UI's agent picker does not offer it; set it through the agents API.

pages.title: HTTP adapter
pages.summary: Trigger an agent that runs as your own service with one HTTP request
pages.firstParagraph: The http adapter sends one HTTP request to a service you run. The service does the work and calls the AgentDash API itself. The web UI's agent picker does not offer it; set it through the agents API.

pages.title: External adapters
pages.summary: Package an adapter on its own and install it into a self-hosted AgentDash instance
pages.firstParagraph: An external adapter is a package outside the AgentDash source tree that the server loads at runtime. It runs agents the same way a built-in adapter does. An instance admin installs it from npm or from a local directory, and the server loads it again at every start.

pages.title: Creating an adapter
pages.summary: Build an adapter that connects AgentDash to another agent runtime
pages.firstParagraph: An adapter connects AgentDash to an agent runtime. Build one when none of the built-in types runs your agent.

pages.title: Adapter UI parser contract
pages.summary: Ship a run-log parser with an external adapter so the AgentDash UI renders its output as a transcript
pages.firstParagraph: The web UI turns each line of an agent's stdout into transcript entries: assistant text, thinking, tool calls, tool results, system lines. Built-in adapters have parsers compiled into the UI. An external adapter can ship its own as ui-parser.js. Without one, the UI uses the…

pages.title: The AgentDash API
pages.summary: What the HTTP API contract covers, what "internal" means, and where to start.
pages.firstParagraph: Everything the web app does, it does through one HTTP API: JSON over HTTPS, under /api on your instance. The CLI, the MCP server and agentdash-connect use the same API. You can too.

pages.title: Authentication
pages.summary: The seven credentials the server accepts, how each is sent, and what each may reach.
pages.firstParagraph: Every request passes through one middleware, server/src/middleware/auth.ts, which turns the credential it carries into an actor: a person (a board actor), an agent, or an enrolled machine. Routes then decide what that actor may do. This page describes that middleware; where it…

pages.title: API keys
pages.summary: Board keys and agent keys — what each can do, how to get one, and how to revoke it.
headings: Minting one: the CLI sign-in flow
The easier way: a connect code
pages.firstParagraph: Two kinds of key are issued to people. A board key acts as you. An agent key acts as one agent. Neither has scopes: a board key can do what you can do, and an agent key can do what its agent can do.

pages.title: Conventions
pages.summary: Ids, request and error format, visibility, pagination and rate limits — as the server implements them.
pages.firstParagraph: What holds for the whole API. Each section names the file it was read from; where a number is given, it is the server's default, read from that file, and an instance's operator can change some of them.

pages.title: Versioning and deprecation
pages.summary: What may change in the API contract and when, how a breaking change is announced, and what internal routes promise.
headings: Changes that ship in any release
Changes that need a deprecation cycle
pages.firstParagraph: The API contract is version v1. Under the policy proposed here, additive changes may ship in any release, and a breaking change to a contract operation will be announced in the release notes at least one stable release before it lands, with the old shape kept working for 60 days…

pages.title: API reference
pages.summary: Every operation in the public API contract, rendered from the OpenAPI 3.1 document.
pages.firstParagraph: Every operation in the contract, with its parameters, request body, responses and the credentials it accepts. It is rendered from docs/api/openapi.yaml, which is generated from the contract manifest and the server's own validators and types — see the overview for how it is kept…

pages.title: Health
pages.summary: Is the server up, which version is it, and are any of its checks degraded.
pages.firstParagraph: GET /api/health tells a load balancer, an install script or a monitor whether the server is answering and whether it can reach its database. It also reports the server version and a few checks that can go degraded: disk space, backup age and stuck runs.

pages.title: Companies
pages.summary: The top-level tenant — list, read, create and update companies.
pages.firstParagraph: A company is the tenant everything else belongs to: its agents, issues, projects, goals, approvals, routines, costs and secrets all carry its id. These operations list the companies you can reach, read one, create a new one, and change its settings.

pages.title: Agents
pages.summary: The AI employees of a company — list and read them, change their settings, pause and resume them, and manage their API keys.
pages.firstParagraph: An agent is one AI employee of a company: it has a name and role, an adapter that runs it, a budget, and a place in the reporting line. These operations list a company's agents, read one, change its settings, pause and resume it, and mint, list and revoke its API keys.

pages.title: Issues
pages.summary: Units of work — list, read, create and update issues, check one out, release it, and comment on it.
pages.firstParagraph: An issue is one unit of work in a company: it has a title, a status, a priority and at most one assignee, an agent or a person. These operations list and read issues, create and change them, let an agent claim one with a checkout and give it back with a release, and read and add…

pages.title: Projects
pages.summary: Groups of issues toward a deliverable — list, read, create and update projects.
pages.firstParagraph: A project groups a company's issues toward one deliverable, and can link to the goals that deliverable serves. These operations list the projects you can see, read one, create one, and change it.

pages.title: Goals
pages.summary: The outcomes a company's work rolls up to — list, read, create and update goals.
pages.firstParagraph: A goal is an outcome the company is working toward; goals nest under a parent goal, and projects link to the goals they serve. Everyone in the company can read its goals, but only an admin can set or change them.

pages.title: Approvals
pages.summary: Requests that wait on a person — list, read, file and decide them.
pages.firstParagraph: An approval is a request that waits on a person: an agent asks to hire another agent, to go past a budget, to send through a connector, or to go ahead with a plan. These operations list and read a company's approvals, file a new one, and approve, reject or send one back for…

pages.title: Routines
pages.summary: Standing instructions that create work on a schedule or on demand — list, read, create, update and run them.
pages.firstParagraph: A routine is a standing instruction: each time it runs, it creates an issue from its title and description and assigns it to an agent. These operations list and read a company's routines, create and change one, and start a run now.

pages.title: Costs
pages.summary: Report what an agent's model calls cost, and read the company's spend in total and per agent.
pages.firstParagraph: Every model call an agent makes can be recorded as a cost event: tokens in and out, the provider and model, and what it cost in cents. These operations report one event and read back two summaries built from them: the company's total against its budget, and the same spend split…

pages.title: Activity
pages.summary: Read a company's activity log — who did what, to which entity, and when.
pages.firstParagraph: The activity log records what happens in a company: an issue created, an agent paused, a secret rotated, a cost reported. This operation reads it, newest first, filtered by agent, by entity or by time.

pages.title: Dashboard
pages.summary: One call for a company's state — agents, issues, this month's spend, pending decisions and recent run health.
pages.firstParagraph: The dashboard summary is the company at a glance: how many agents are working, how much work is open, what this month has cost, and what is waiting on a person. It is one read, computed when you ask for it, and the web app's home page is built from it.

pages.title: Secrets
pages.summary: Store a company secret, list secrets by name, and rotate a value. Values are never returned.
headings: Using a secret in agent configuration
pages.firstParagraph: A secret is a named value, such as an API key, that agents use without it ever appearing in their configuration. You store the value once; agent configuration refers to the secret by id, and the server puts the value into the agent's environment when a run starts.

pages.title: Human control
pages.summary: A named person's board key discovers, reads, prepares and confirms a finite set of versioned operations.
pages.firstParagraph: Human control lets a person act through their own board key — usually from a local MCP client — using a fixed list of versioned operations instead of arbitrary API calls. Reads answer directly; every change is prepared first, shown back to the person in full, and runs only when…

pages.title: Bridge
pages.summary: How an enrolled machine claims a task, returns its result, or declines it.
pages.firstParagraph: The bridge lets agents hand work to a person's own machine. The machine asks for the next task, does it locally, and answers with a result or a refusal. The server never connects to the machine.

pages.title: MCP endpoints
pages.summary: The two Model Context Protocol endpoints — one for an agent key, one for an assistant's OAuth grant.
pages.firstParagraph: The instance serves the Model Context Protocol over streamable HTTP at two paths. POST /api/mcp takes an agent key and serves that agent's tools. POST /api/mcp/assistant takes an OAuth access token and serves an assistant's tools for one person.

pages.title: OAuth metadata
pages.summary: The public discovery documents an assistant client reads to find the instance's OAuth endpoints.
pages.firstParagraph: An assistant that connects to POST /api/mcp/assistant gets its access token through OAuth 2.1. These three documents tell the client where to get one. They are public, take no credential, and are served at the app root, not under /api.

pages.title: API changelog
pages.summary: The API-affecting lines of every AgentDash release note, newest first. Generated from releases/*.md.
pages.firstParagraph: Generated from releases/.md by scripts/docs/generate-api-changelog.mjs: 53 lines from 15 releases, out of 24 AgentDash releases read. A line is kept when it names an /api/… path or a method and path, a contract operation, a status code, a header, a validator, or the words route,…

pages.title: Route index
pages.summary: Every HTTP route the server registers, generated from the route files. Only routes marked as in the contract are promised.
pages.firstParagraph: Measured: 608 routes in 81 route files under server/src/routes/, counted by scripts/docs/generate-route-index.mjs from each router.( call and resolved against the mounts in server/src/app.ts. Route-list digest bf3a4cc1aba8; it changes exactly when a route is added, removed,…

pages.title: MCP overview
pages.summary: The AgentDash MCP server, its transports and toolsets, and where each reference page comes from.
pages.firstParagraph: AgentDash serves the Model Context Protocol from one server, packages/mcp-server. A harness reaches it over stdio (the agentdash-mcp binary, packages/mcp-server/src/stdio.ts) or over streamable HTTP on the instance itself: POST /api/mcp with an agent key, and POST…

pages.title: Connecting
pages.summary: stdio, streamable HTTP with an agent key, and OAuth 2.1 for assistants — and what agentdash-connect writes.
headings: Streamable HTTP with an agent key
pages.firstParagraph: There are three ways in. The credential you hold decides which one applies.

pages.title: Toolsets
pages.summary: What each MCP toolset is for, who gets it, and how a connection's toolset is chosen.
